question: What is a major goal of physical therapy in the long-term management of a child with spastic cerebral palsy?

options.A: Eliminating the need for any assistive devices by age five
options.B: Preventing joint contractures and improving functional mobility
options.C: Permanently stopping all involuntary muscle contractions
options.D: Curing the underlying brain lesion through intense exercise

explanation: Physical therapy uses stretching, strengthening, and positioning to keep muscles pliable and prevent permanent joint tightening. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T4#GNS324_U4_T4_h6)

question: Why does a patient often experience bad chills right before their temperature shoots up with a fever?

options.A: The kidneys are failing to filter out toxic waste products
options.B: The nervous system is reacting to a sudden drop in room temperature
options.C: Blood vessels are dilating to release trapped heat from the skin
options.D: The muscles are rapidly contracting to generate internal heat

explanation: Exactly! Shivering is just your muscles moving quickly to build up warmth so your body can reach its new, higher fever setting.

question: What is another popular name for the ductus deferens?

options.A: Urethral tube
options.B: Vas deferens
options.C: Ejaculatory canal
options.D: Seminiferous duct

explanation: You will hear clinical instructors and textbooks use 'ductus deferens' and 'vas deferens' interchangeably. They are the exact same tube!

question: During which phase of the nurse-patient relationship do you first build trust and set professional boundaries?

options.A: The termination phase
options.B: The working phase
options.C: The pre-interaction phase
options.D: The orientation phase

explanation: The orientation phase is your official 'meet and greet' where you introduce yourself, set ground rules, explain your roles, and start building that vital therapeutic trust.

question: When nurses interview local leaders and hold listening sessions during a community assessment, what kind of information are they gathering?

options.A: Qualitative insights
options.B: Quantitative statistics
options.C: Pharmacological logs
options.D: Genomic sequences

explanation: You've got this! Interviews and listening sessions give you qualitative data—meaning the real stories, lived experiences, and personal views of community members that numbers alone can't show.

question: What is the main reason a hospital reviews things after an adverse event happens?

options.A: To increase the cost of patient care services
options.B: To prove that the hospital was not at fault
options.C: To identify which specific nurse to terminate
options.D: To redesign workplace workflows and prevent the same event from happening again

explanation: Well done! Mistakes teach us how to fix our systems so the same thing never happens to another patient.

question: How is the BCG vaccine usually given to a newborn?

options.A: Subcutaneously in the thigh
options.B: Intradermally into the skin
options.C: Orally using liquid drops
options.D: Deep intramuscular injection

explanation: Correct! BCG goes just under the top layer of skin (intradermally), usually on the upper left arm, leaving a small bump that later turns into a scar.

question: Which lab test must be checked regularly for a patient on testosterone replacement therapy?

options.A: Prostate-specific antigen
options.B: Fastin blood glucose
options.C: Serum creatinine levels
options.D: White blood cell count

explanation: We keep an eye on prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels because extra testosterone can encourage the prostate to grow.

question: How does untreated cervicitis affect a patient's risk of contracting HIV?

options.A: It grants temporary immunity against sexually transmitted viruses.
options.B: It decreases the risk because white blood cells destroy the virus.
options.C: It increases the risk because the mucosal tissue is broken and immune cells are rushed to the area.
options.D: It has no measurable impact on viral transmission rates.

explanation: Inflamed, fragile tissue plus a gathering of immune cells gives viruses like HIV an easier pathway into the body.

question: A nurse accidentally types a patient's heart rate as 12 instead of 120 beats per minute. What primary concept does this error affect?

options.A: Physical network security
options.B: Data quality and validity
options.C: Patient financial billing status
options.D: Hospital building architecture

explanation: Typo alerts happen, but entering the wrong numbers ruins the trustworthiness and accuracy of the patient's official health record. Always double-check your vitals! [learn more](GNS113_U2_T5#GNS113_U2_T5_h5)

question: A patient on a new psychiatric drug is refusing to eat due to severe dry mouth. Who should the nurse consult first?

options.A: The medical records coding and billing department
options.B: The registered dietitian and the prescribing psychiatrist
options.C: The hospital maintenance and facility management team
options.D: The security personnel assigned to the psychiatric unit

explanation: You got it! A dietitian can help modify food textures for dry mouth, while the psychiatrist can review the medication dosage.

question: What do we call a specific patch of skin that gets its nerve supply from just one spinal nerve?

options.A: Ganglion
options.B: Funiculus
options.C: Myotome
options.D: Dermatome

explanation: Brilliant! A dermatome is just a skin map. 'Derma' means skin, and each segment corresponds to a specific spinal nerve pair checking in on that area.

question: What is the big advantage of partnering with local transport unions during a disaster?

options.A: Financing the national budget for disaster management
options.B: Securing vehicles quickly for evacuation and relief supply delivery
options.C: Exempting commercial drivers from all traffic laws permanently
options.D: Allowing union members to take over government leadership roles

explanation: Spot on! Transport unions have plenty of vehicles and know the local shortcuts, which speeds up evacuations and getting supplies where they need to go.

question: What is the main lifelong treatment needed for someone with Type 1 diabetes?

options.A: Lifelong insulin therapy
options.B: Temporary blood thinners
options.C: Oral metformin tablets only
options.D: Weekly antibiotic injections

explanation: Since the body isn't making insulin at all in Type 1, patients must take insulin every day to survive. You're doing great with your pharmacology basics!

question: A massive passenger train crash is classified under which type of disaster?

options.A: Technological Industrial Leaks
options.B: Transportation Disasters
options.C: Biological Contaminations
options.D: Natural Weather Anomalies

explanation: You got it! Accidents involving mass transport like trains, planes, and large buses are grouped as transportation disasters.

question: What is a major role of state-level primary health care bodies in Nigeria?

options.A: Building private international airports
options.B: Collecting local market taxes for traditional rulers
options.C: Appointing village chiefs in rural communities
options.D: Supervising LGA activities and procuring bulk medical supplies

explanation: State bodies provide mid-level oversight, supporting local governments with supplies, training, and technical guidance. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T7#GNS124_U1_T7_h5)

question: What is the main purpose of a clinical audit in a hospital?

options.A: Comparing current nursing practice against established standards
options.B: Counting the number of visitors on a ward
options.C: Calculating the monthly salary of nursing staff
options.D: Checking the expiration dates of food in the canteen

explanation: A clinical audit is simply checking our actual bedside practice against the golden standard of care to see how well we are doing.

question: How does using the System of Profound Knowledge change how a nurse views a medication error on the ward?

options.A: It proves human error can be completely stopped if staff try harder.
options.B: It shifts focus from blaming the nurse to fixing flaws in the medication process.
options.C: It helps calculate the exact financial cost to the hospital.
options.D: It decides the best disciplinary action for the staff involved.

explanation: Great nursing management is all about fixing the system so humans can succeed, rather than pointing fingers when mistakes happen!

question: Why don't we diagnose someone with high blood pressure (hypertension) after just one high reading?

options.A: Nigerian guidelines require at least five months of tracking
options.B: Blood pressure machines only work accurately on the third try
options.C: Systolic pressure changes constantly based on what food was eaten
options.D: Temporary factors like stress or rushing can falsely raise readings

explanation: Things like rushing to the clinic, traffic anxiety, or pain can make BP jump temporarily. That's why we always check a few times before making a diagnosis. Great job thinking like a nurse!

question: A nurse researcher wants to measure patient satisfaction in the most detailed way possible. Which option should they choose?

options.A: Asking patients to answer simply yes or no to being satisfied
options.B: Using a continuous numerical rating scale from zero to one hundred
options.C: Grouping patients into satisfied, neutral, or dissatisfied categories
options.D: Classifying hospital units by their primary nursing delivery model

explanation: A 0-100 rating gives you rich, detailed numbers instead of forcing patients into simple yes/no boxes. Great job working through these!

question: What is conflict primarily viewed as in a modern healthcare setting?

options.A: An inevitable part of a busy work environment
options.B: A personal failure of the nurse manager
options.C: An illegal workplace violation
options.D: A definite sign of a failing nursing unit

explanation: Because healthcare brings together many busy professionals under high stress, conflict naturally happens and is expected. [learn more](GST321_U5_T3#GST321_U5_T3_h1)

question: Why do we always keep raw meat separate from ready-to-eat foods?

options.A: To speed up the cooking process
options.B: To improve the overall taste of the meal
options.C: To reduce the financial cost of cooking
options.D: To prevent cross-contamination of harmful bacteria

explanation: Think of it like keeping bad company away from good! Separating raw meat stops dangerous germs from jumping onto foods that won't be cooked again before eating.

question: Which of the following is NOT a good practice when conducting community health education?

options.A: Involving respected local leaders in the mobilization
options.B: Addressing local cultural beliefs respectfully
options.C: Using complex medical jargon to impress the audience
options.D: Communicating in the primary language of the community

explanation: Using complicated clinical terms confuses people and creates a barrier to learning, which is why simple language is essential. [learn more](GNS225_U2_T4#GNS225_U2_T4_h7)

question: Why are prophylactic antibiotics usually given within one hour before the surgical incision is made?

options.A: To allow the surgical team time to perform hand scrubbing rituals
options.B: To neutralize any bacteria already present in the circulating air
options.C: To prevent the patient from experiencing nausea while on the operating table
options.D: To ensure peak tissue concentration of the drug when the skin is opened

explanation: Timing is everything! Giving the drug right before surgery means the antibiotic is fully active in the tissues the exact second the skin opens.

question: What is a key question a nurse can ask to assess food security in a patient?

options.A: What is your exact family income down to the last dollar?
options.B: Do you prefer eating white bread or whole grain bread?
options.C: Do you worry about running out of food before getting more money?
options.D: How many hours of physical exercise do you do each week?

explanation: Screening for food security involves asking direct, simple questions about running out of food and lacking money to buy more. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T020#GNS227_U2_T020_h8)

question: What is the main job of glucose inside Oral Rehydration Salts (ORS)?

options.A: It masks the salty taste of the solution for infants
options.B: It slows down the movement of food through the stomach
options.C: It provides all the daily calories a sick child needs
options.D: It helps transport sodium and water across the intestinal wall

explanation: It's like a buddy system! Glucose hitches a ride with sodium and water, pulling them across the intestinal wall back into the bloodstream to stop dehydration.

question: A patient needs a nasogastric tube but has a history of a severe skull fracture at the base of the head. What should you do?

options.A: Perform the insertion quickly while the patient is asleep
options.B: Proceed with normal insertion using extra lubrication
options.C: Consult the doctor because putting a tube through the nose is risky here
options.D: Insert the tube through the mouth instead without checking

explanation: A basilar skull fracture means the bone near the brain is damaged, so passing a tube through the nose could accidentally enter the brain. Always check with your senior or doctor!

question: Why might a doctor order a CA-125 blood test for a patient with an ovarian mass?

options.A: To diagnose a sudden bacterial infection in the pelvis
options.B: To check if the patient is currently pregnant
options.C: To help check for markers associated with ovarian cancer
options.D: To measure the exact amount of estrogen in the blood

explanation: CA-125 is just a protein marker in the blood that can go up when certain ovarian growths are present. It helps doctors get a clearer picture!

question: Which of these is one of the classic stages of grief identified by Elisabeth Kübler-Ross?

options.A: Detachment
options.B: Bargaining
options.C: Resolution
options.D: Isolation

explanation: Spot on! Bargaining is a well-known stage where a person tries to negotiate a way out of the painful reality, like saying 'God, if you heal them, I will change my ways.'

question: A researcher spots a few strange blood pressure numbers that look like typos in the database. What is the best first step?

options.A: Ignore the mistakes and run the statistical analysis anyway
options.B: Change the numbers randomly to fit the average reading
options.C: Check the original paper records to verify the correct entry
options.D: Delete all the patient records so they do not ruin the study

explanation: Data cleaning means checking suspicious entries against original source documents rather than guessing or deleting data carelessly.

question: Why is a woman's fertile window wider than just the single day she ovulates?

options.A: Eggs can remain fertile in the fallopian tubes for nearly a week.
options.B: Sperm can survive inside the female reproductive tract for up to five days.
options.C: Hormones remain elevated for a full week after ovulation.
options.D: Multiple eggs are released over several days during every cycle.

explanation: Sperm are remarkably resilient! Because they can hang out in the female tract for up to five days, intercourse days before ovulation can still lead to pregnancy.

question: What are the two main cavities that divide the inside of the human body?

options.A: dorsal and ventral body cavities
options.B: thoracic and abdominopelvic cavities
options.C: serous and mucous membrane layers
options.D: cranial and spinal body regions

explanation: You've got this! The human body splits its main internal spaces into the dorsal cavity at the back and the ventral cavity at the front.

question: Which of these activities counts toward Nigeria's GDP?

options.A: A Nigerian nurse working in a London hospital
options.B: A retired Nigerian citizen receiving a pension abroad
options.C: A foreign company manufacturing drugs entirely overseas
options.D: A foreign doctor treating patients at a private clinic in Lagos

explanation: You've got this! Because the medical service takes place physically inside Nigeria, it contributes to Nigeria's GDP.

question: What is spermatogenesis?

options.A: The release of seminal fluid during ejaculation
options.B: The storage of mature sperm inside the epididymis
options.C: The hormonal control of secondary sex characteristics
options.D: The production of mature sperm cells from primitive germ cells

explanation: Spermatogenesis describes the biological creation and development of mature sperm cells from immature precursors in the testes. [learn more](GNS216_U2_T7#GNS216_U2_T7_h1)

question: Which clinical sign tells you a patient is slipping into dangerous septic shock?

options.A: Localized redness and swelling around a surgical incision
options.B: High white blood cell count without any fever present
options.C: Dangerously low blood pressure unresponsive to fluids
options.D: Increased urine output caused by excessive fluid intake

explanation: Spot on! In septic shock, blood vessels relax so much that blood pressure plummets dangerously low and stubbornly refuses to bounce back, even after giving IV fluids.

question: How would you simply describe an autoimmune disease?

options.A: A condition where the immune system attacks the body's own healthy tissues
options.B: A temporary infection spread through close contact in a community
options.C: An immediate allergic reaction caused by exposure to environmental pollen
options.D: A genetic deficiency that prevents the production of red blood cells

explanation: In autoimmune diseases, the immune system gets confused and mistakenly treats friendly, healthy body cells as enemies, attacking them by mistake.

question: Why do dangerous heart rhythms (arrhythmias) often cause a sudden drop in blood flow?

options.A: The coronary arteries squeeze shut and stop all blood to the lungs
options.B: The heart valves instantly fuse shut and block all movement
options.C: The heart chambers do not fill and squeeze in an orderly sequence
options.D: The electrical signals travel way too slowly down normal pathways

explanation: When the heart beats chaotically or too fast, it flutters instead of squeezing properly. Without teamwork between filling and pumping, blood just doesn't move.

question: Why is it usually unfair and unhelpful to immediately blame an individual nurse when a clinical mistake happens?

options.A: It forces the patient to leave the healthcare facility prematurely
options.B: It automatically increases the financial budget of the hospital ward
options.C: It violates international nursing licensing laws instantly
options.D: It ignores underlying system and psychological factors that caused the mistake

explanation: Most mistakes happen because of faulty systems or rushed environments, not because a nurse doesn't care. Fixing the system stops the error from happening again!

question: Which ventilator mode gives a set volume when the patient tries to breathe, but also guarantees a minimum backup rate if they get too tired?

options.A: Control mode
options.B: Assist-Control mode
options.C: Continuous Positive Airway Pressure
options.D: Pressure Support mode

explanation: In Assist-Control mode, the machine is always watching: if the patient breathes, the machine helps out with a full breath. If the patient stops trying, the machine's timer steps in to breathe for them!

question: A patient tagged as yellow suddenly starts gasping for air and showing signs of shock. What should you do?

options.A: Ask the patient to walk over to the green area
options.B: Leave the patient in the yellow category because triage tags never change
options.C: Re-tag the patient as red and provide immediate life-saving care
options.D: Move the patient to the black category immediately

explanation: Triage isn't a one-time thing; patient conditions change fast! If someone gets worse, you upgrade their tag right away to get them urgent help.

question: What is the maximum window of time to start Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP) after a potential HIV exposure?

options.A: 1 week
options.B: 12 minutes
options.C: 72 hours
options.D: 24 days

explanation: That's right! PEP works best when started right away and must be taken within 72 hours to stop the virus from taking hold.

question: Why do cystine stones form much faster when the urine is acidic?

options.A: Acidic conditions accelerate the speed of the glomerular filtration rate
options.B: Low pH causes the kidneys to manufacture more amino acids
options.C: Cystine has very poor solubility at a low pH level
options.D: Acidic urine destroys the protective lining of the renal pelvis

explanation: Cystine doesn't like to dissolve in acid! When urine is acidic, cystine clumps together instead of staying dissolved, turning into stubborn little crystals and stones.

question: How does the poliovirus mainly spread from person to person?

options.A: Vector-borne mosquito bites
options.B: Fecal-oral route
options.C: Direct sexual contact
options.D: Aerosol droplet inhalation

explanation: You've got this! The virus usually spreads when someone unknowingly eats or drinks something contaminated with tiny amounts of infected waste matter.

question: A newly diagnosed patient tells you, 'The lab results are mixed up; I feel fine!' Which stage of grief is this?

options.A: Acceptance
options.B: Denial
options.C: Bargaining
options.D: Anger

explanation: Spot on! Refusing to believe a scary diagnosis is a classic way patients protect themselves from sudden emotional shock.

question: To prove nursing negligence in a legal case, four elements must be present. Which of these is NOT one of them?

options.A: A legally recognized duty of care to the patient
options.B: Intentional malice or hatred from the nurse
options.C: Actual injury or damage suffered by the patient
options.D: A direct link between the nurse's action and the injury

explanation: You nailed it! Negligence doesn't mean you wanted to hurt someone; it's about carelessness or an oversight that broke the standard of care.

question: Why must nurses monitor vital signs very closely in a patient with a suspected brainstem injury involving the medulla?

options.A: Cardiovascular and respiratory failure can happen suddenly
options.B: Kidney failure develops within the first hour
options.C: Blood pressure medications stop working entirely
options.D: Core body temperature always drops below normal

explanation: Because the medulla houses the primary breathing and heart rate centers, injury here directly threatens life support functions. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T21#GNS211_U3_T21_h6)

question: A patient has a cough that gets worse during workdays but clears up completely on weekends. What should you suspect?

options.A: An acute infection caught during weekend travel
options.B: A symptom unrelated to lifestyle or environment
options.C: An occupational exposure in the work environment
options.D: A purely genetic heart condition

explanation: When symptoms flare up only during work hours and ease during rest days, it's a huge clue that something at work is causing it.

question: Which type of dietary fiber is best known for adding bulk to stool and keeping things moving smoothly in the gut?

options.A: Simple fiber
options.B: Glycogen fiber
options.C: Soluble fiber
options.D: Insoluble fiber

explanation: Spot on! Insoluble fiber doesn't break down easily, so it adds bulk and helps prevent constipation.

question: Why is it smart to check back on a patient shortly after giving them a new intravenous drug?

options.A: To ask if they want extra hospital bed sheets
options.B: To remind the patient to pay their hospital treatment bills
options.C: To collect the empty plastic tray and disposable syringe
options.D: To check for immediate adverse reactions or allergic responses

explanation: IV drugs act fast! Popping back in lets you catch sudden allergic reactions or low blood pressure early when you can easily help.

question: Where does the vast majority of tubular reabsorption take place within the nephron?

options.A: Glomerular capsule
options.B: Proximal convoluted tubule
options.C: Distal convoluted tubule
options.D: Collecting duct

explanation: The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs the largest share of filtered water, glucose, and essential ions back into the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS121_U2_T5#GNS121_U2_T5_h6)

question: Why is verifying a patient's identity critical during a tele-nursing consultation?

options.A: To ensure the patient is using an approved brand of mobile phone
options.B: To prevent unauthorized persons from receiving confidential health information
options.C: To confirm that the patient has paid their hospital utility bills
options.D: To make sure the patient's internet connection speed is fast enough

explanation: Identity verification protects patient privacy and ensures sensitive medical details are not disclosed to the wrong party. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T12#GNS212_U4_T12_h4)

question: What is the main purpose of nursing orientation when starting at a new hospital?

options.A: To discipline nurses who break minor hospital uniform rules
options.B: To determine the annual leave days for all hospital staff
options.C: To introduce the employee to policies, layout, and team culture
options.D: To test the clinical speed of experienced foreign nurses

explanation: Orientation helps you find your way around, meet your new colleagues, and learn how things are done in that specific hospital so you feel right at home.

question: Which of these is classified as a modern contraceptive method?

options.A: Subdermal implants
options.B: Withdrawal method
options.C: Periodic abstinence
options.D: Calendar tracking

explanation: Implants are modern medical methods! Methods like withdrawal and tracking the calendar are traditional practices rather than modern medical interventions.

question: What chemical feature makes a fatty acid 'saturated'?

options.A: It only comes from plant sources
options.B: It stays completely liquid at room temperature
options.C: It has no double bonds between carbon atoms
options.D: It has multiple double bonds in the chain

explanation: Saturated fats are packed tightly together with single bonds only, which is why butter (a saturated fat) stays solid at room temperature!

question: A patient suddenly feels a strong need to pee and leaks a little before reaching the toilet. What is this called?

options.A: Urinary incontinence
options.B: Hematuria
options.C: Renal failure
options.D: Urinary retention

explanation: Incontinence simply means losing control of urine flow. You will see this a lot in clinical rotations!

question: Why is it super important for bedside nurses to have a voice when testing new hospital software?

options.A: To ensure the tools match real-world clinical workflows and needs
options.B: To take over hospital information technology department jobs
options.C: To eliminate the need for clinical supervisors and managers
options.D: To learn computer programming and software coding languages

explanation: You got it! Nobody knows the hustle of the ward better than nurses. Our feedback ensures new tech actually helps us care for patients instead of getting in our way.

question: A patient with severe preeclampsia suddenly stops passing urine and shows signs of fluid overload. What should you do first as the nurse?

options.A: Encourage her to drink large volumes of oral water to flush the kidneys
options.B: Administer oral diuretics without a doctor's order to force urination
options.C: Monitor for respiratory distress and report failing urine output immediately
options.D: Prepare the patient for immediate home discharge with dietary advice

explanation: Not peeing plus fluid overload is an urgent red flag! Fluid can back up into the lungs, so reporting this immediately can save a life.

question: Why is time considered so critical when dealing with emergency medical conditions?

options.A: Hospital regulations require fast bed turnover
options.B: Insurance companies will not pay for slow care
options.C: Doctors refuse to see patients who wait too long
options.D: Delays can lead to rapid deterioration and death

explanation: In critical emergencies, minutes matter because a failing body system quickly causes permanent harm or death if not supported. [learn more](GNS315_U2_T2#GNS315_U2_T2_h1)

question: Which activity is commonly included in the daily routine of a half-way house?

options.A: Intensive major surgery training workshops
options.B: Strict solitary confinement in locked rooms
options.C: Mandatory bed rest for twenty-four hours
options.D: Shared morning chores and group meetings

explanation: Spot on! Daily schedules feature teamwork activities like shared chores and meetings to encourage social interaction and cooperation.

question: Which group of people needs extra protection and care in nursing research?

options.A: Staff registered nurses
options.B: Prisoners and children
options.C: Hospital chief executive officers
options.D: Experienced clinical instructors

explanation: Spot on! Children, prisoners, and unconscious patients need extra ethical safeguards because they might not be fully free to say yes or no. [learn more](GNS217_U3_T13#GNS217_U3_T13_h6)

question: Which body problem is a very common cause of sudden confusion or unconsciousness?

options.A: Severe hypoglycemia
options.B: A ruptured cerebral aneurysm
options.C: Bacterial meningitis
options.D: A penetrating skull fracture

explanation: Spot on! When blood sugar drops too low (hypoglycemia), the brain gets starved of its main energy source and shuts down fast.

question: How far should an adult rectal suppository be inserted past the anal sphincter by the nurse?

options.A: All the way into the ascending colon
options.B: Just inside the outer skin folds
options.C: 2.5 to 5 centimeters
options.D: 10 to 12 centimeters

explanation: Inserting it 2.5 to 5 cm past the internal sphincter ensures the medication stays in place and does not slip right back out. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T18#GNS125_U3_T18_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of advance care planning?

options.A: To allow patients to state their medical wishes before they lose decision-making capacity
options.B: To reduce hospital liability in case of accidental patient falls
options.C: To guarantee that a patient receives aggressive life support under all circumstances
options.D: To transfer financial assets to family members before passing away

explanation: Advance care planning lets individuals guide their future healthcare treatment when they are no longer able to speak or make decisions for themselves. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T13#GNS321_U4_T13_h6)

question: What is a major social challenge faced by half-way houses in Nigeria?

options.A: Excessive public demand for luxury hotel-style rooms
options.B: Stigma leading to community resistance against facility locations
options.C: Too many trained psychiatrists wanting to work in the homes
options.D: An overabundance of government funding and free resources

explanation: True. Deep-seated cultural stigma often makes neighbors uneasy or resistant when a mental health facility tries to open in their neighborhood.

question: A ward manager notices high rates of patient falls. Which QA objective is most relevant to addressing this?

options.A: Lowering drug costs
options.B: Risk reduction
options.C: Increasing admission rates
options.D: Expanding ward capacity

explanation: When we spot hazards like patient falls, our main goal is risk reduction—taking smart steps to protect our patients from getting hurt on the ward.

question: Which of these is NOT a normal way that toxic substances cause a medical emergency?

options.A: Disrupting cellular oxygen use at the tissue level
options.B: Blocking the normal electrical signals of the heart
options.C: Stimulating the production of healthy bone marrow cells
options.D: Causing sudden and profound systemic vasodilation

explanation: Making healthy blood cells in the bone marrow is a good, normal process! Toxins cause harm by damaging systems, not by boosting healthy growth.

question: Why is it important for a researcher to list study limitations in the discussion?

options.A: To give critics an easy way to reject the paper from journals
options.B: To lengthen the article so it meets minimum word counts
options.C: To show transparency and acknowledge boundaries of the findings
options.D: To prove that the research methods used were completely flawless

explanation: Great job! Every study has weak spots. Being open about them shows you are a thoughtful, honest nurse researcher.

question: What is caregiver burnout?

options.A: An allergic reaction to cleaning supplies used in the home
options.B: Physical and emotional exhaustion caused by prolonged caregiving stress
options.C: A sudden medical illness caught from a patient in the hospital
options.D: The legal termination of a home health care contract

explanation: Caregiver burnout happens when family or informal caregivers become overwhelmed by the continuous physical and emotional demands of supporting a relative. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T4#GNS324_U5_T4_h4)

question: If a displaced community is staying in a crowded makeshift camp after a flood, what health threat should the nurse expect next?

options.A: Immediate reduction in baseline community trauma rates
options.B: Rapid spread of waterborne and communicable diseases
options.C: Sudden widespread outbreaks of genetic blood disorders
options.D: Total elimination of chronic lifestyle health conditions

explanation: When people are crowded together with poor sanitation, infectious diseases can spread very quickly. Nurses play a huge role in preventing this!

question: Why might a client feel dizzy or shaky immediately after completing a Glucose Tolerance Test?

options.A: The client has been deprived of clean drinking water for over 24 hours
options.B: A sudden surge of insulin can cause a temporary drop in blood sugar
options.C: Drawing multiple blood samples removes too many red blood cells
options.D: The concentrated sugar solution causes sudden dehydration of the brain

explanation: The large glucose load prompts an insulin spike that can overshoot and drop blood sugar below normal baseline levels, causing shakiness. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T20#GNS222_U2_T20_h7)

question: What kind of information do you mainly gather when taking a patient's health history?

options.A: Subjective data from the patient
options.B: Quantitative data from vital signs
options.C: Measurable signs from physical exams
options.D: Objective data from laboratory tests

explanation: Spot on! A health history is all about what the patient tells you they are feeling. That makes it subjective data.

question: Why do researchers need to narrow down a massive topic like 'hospital stress'?

options.A: Broad topics are too massive and vague to study effectively all at once
options.B: Patients refuse to talk about general topics
options.C: Narrowing a topic increases the financial cost of the study
options.D: Broad topics are illegal to research in clinical settings

explanation: If your topic is as big as the ocean, you'll drown in data! Narrowing it down gives you a specific pool you can easily swim across.

question: When are your kidneys most likely to start producing extra glucose?

options.A: Prolonged fasting or starvation
options.B: Excessive intake of dietary water
options.C: A sudden spike in blood pressure
options.D: Eating a large carbohydrate-rich meal

explanation: Exactly right! When liver energy stores run out during a long fast, the kidneys step up and make glucose to help keep your body fueled.

question: You examine a child in a rural clinic and notice dry eyes and Bitot's spots. What deficiency should you suspect?

options.A: Vitamin C
options.B: Iron
options.C: Vitamin A
options.D: Calcium

explanation: Dry eyes and Bitot's spots are textbook signs of a Vitamin A deficiency. Great clinical catch!

question: What defense mechanism is happening when someone takes their frustration out on a safer, less threatening target?

options.A: Rationalization
options.B: Denial
options.C: Displacement
options.D: Projection

explanation: Ever had a tough day with a strict lecturer and ended up snapping at your roommate? That's displacement—redirecting your feelings to someone safer. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T15#GNS123_U3_T15_h6)

question: What is the quickest, most reliable daily check to see if a patient is retaining fluid or losing too much?

options.A: Taking blood pressure every hour
options.B: Getting an accurate daily body weight
options.C: Checking the color of their fingernails
options.D: Checking how much food they ate

explanation: Think of it this way: a liter of fluid weighs about a kilo! Daily weights are your best tool to catch sudden fluid changes early.

question: What makes farming pesticides particularly dangerous in rural areas?

options.A: Farmers use them exclusively as food flavoring agents in local dishes
options.B: They are frequently stored near food items and handled without protective gear
options.C: They only affect animals and have zero toxic impact on human physiology
options.D: They lose their toxicity completely within a few minutes of application

explanation: Spot on! When chemicals are kept close to food and used without gloves or masks, accidental poisoning happens easily.

question: A nurse is teaching mothers about ORS preparation. Instead of just lecturing, she asks a mother to come forward and mix the solution herself. Which learning principle is the nurse using?

options.A: Strict isolation
options.B: Punitive correction
options.C: Passive observation
options.D: Active participation

explanation: Having the learner perform the task herself ensures she understands the steps through hands-on practice rather than just listening. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T1#GNS214_U1_T1_h3)

question: Which of the following is a classic example of an obstetric emergency?

options.A: Severe postpartum hemorrhage
options.B: Chronic knee osteoarthritis
options.C: A mild seasonal allergy
options.D: Routine pregnancy checkup

explanation: Heavy bleeding after childbirth is a life-threatening emergency unique to obstetric care. [learn more](GNS315_U2_T1#GNS315_U2_T1_h4)

question: During a severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis, what mainly causes the airway to block?

options.A: Collapse of a main artery in the chest
options.B: Swelling in the throat and tight airways in the lungs
options.C: Paralysis of the diaphragm from fever
options.D: A buildup of thick yellow mucus in the stomach

explanation: The throat swells up and the small breathing tubes in the lungs squeeze shut, making it hard to breathe air in.

question: Why is the postpartum uterine cavity so easily invaded by bacteria?

options.A: Gastric acid production increases significantly during labor
options.B: The cervix remains completely dilated for several months
options.C: Normal flora inside the uterus becomes entirely pathogenic
options.D: The placental site is a large, raw, vascular wound

explanation: Think of where the placenta detached—it leaves behind a large, healing wound with open blood vessels. This makes it a very easy pathway for bacteria to enter.

question: Why do some parasites practice 'antigenic variation' (changing their outer coats)?

options.A: To change its outer proteins and evade the host immune response
options.B: To attract more vectors for spreading to a new host
options.C: To help the parasite burrow faster through skin layers
options.D: To increase the speed at which it digests host nutrients

explanation: Clever parasite! By constantly changing their outer appearance, they trick the immune system into not recognizing them, dodging attacks.

question: You realize you forgot to document a vital medication given two hours ago. What should you do?

options.A: Leave it out entirely because late charting is illegal
options.B: Write a late entry clearly labeled with the current time and the actual time of the event
options.C: Wait until the end of the month and add it to the file
options.D: Squeeze the note between previous lines and backdate your signature

explanation: Spot on! Always write a clear 'late entry' with the correct times. Never backdate or try to squeeze notes between lines.

question: A community health nurse in a rural Nigerian village organizes an outreach to teach mothers how to mix oral rehydration salts for diarrhea. What type of intervention is this?

options.A: A purely administrative task unrelated to patient welfare
options.B: A tertiary action meant exclusively for chronic surgical patients
options.C: An unnecessary hospital procedure reserved only for intensive care units
options.D: A practical community-level nursing intervention promoting health recovery

explanation: Community outreach brings essential health knowledge directly to where people live to prevent severe illness. [learn more](GNS123_U1_T5#GNS123_U1_T5_h6)

question: What is the main purpose of taking a nutrition history in nursing practice?

options.A: To gather information about a patient's food intake and eating habits
options.B: To strictly calculate the exact daily financial cost of groceries
options.C: To diagnose rare genetic metabolic disorders immediately
options.D: To prescribe specific medical diets without consulting a doctor

explanation: A nutrition history focuses directly on understanding what and how a patient eats to guide their care. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T002#GNS227_U5_T002_h1)

question: What do we call an infectious disease that jumps naturally from animals to humans?

options.A: Nosocomial infection
options.B: Idiopathic disease
options.C: Opportunistic pathogen
options.D: Zoonosis

explanation: A zoonotic disease (or zoonosis) is an infection that normally lives in animals but can cross over to infect humans.

question: If a patient is stable and suddenly starts getting worse during an ABCDEF check, what should the team do right away?

options.A: Rush the patient to the operating theatre
options.B: Go straight back to step A and check the airway again
options.C: Finish the rest of the protocol steps first
options.D: Wait at the bedside for the doctor to arrive

explanation: Spot on! If a patient takes a turn for the worse, always cycle right back to the beginning (Airway) to catch any new breathing or airway trouble. Excellent clinical thinking!

question: Why is 24-hour accountability so important in primary nursing?

options.A: It ensures consistent, uninterrupted planning and evaluation of patient care across all shifts.
options.B: It forces the primary nurse to stay awake in the hospital for a full day and night.
options.C: It guarantees that physicians do not need to visit the patient after admission.
options.D: It prevents associate nurses from ever touching the patient or charting notes.

explanation: Don't worry, nurses don't stay awake 24 hours! 24-hour accountability means the primary nurse sets the master plan so that even when they go home to rest, other shifts follow that same smooth path.

question: Why is the teach-back method especially useful when teaching clients with low health literacy?

options.A: It proves that the client has memorized complex medical terminology
options.B: It replaces the need for any non-verbal communication techniques
options.C: It confirms whether the client truly understood the instructions in their own words
options.D: It tests the nurse's ability to speak multiple foreign languages

explanation: Having clients repeat instructions in their own words ensures they grasp the care plan and catches any misunderstandings early. [learn more](GNS225_U2_T22#GNS225_U2_T22_h7)
